newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-Polish NBP seeks help to cool credit boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Polish NBP seeks help to cool credit boom.

text.p: Poland's central bank on Tuesday called on the country's left-wing government to balance the 1998 budget or risk a Czech-style financial crisis, but the government dismissed its advice.

In a newspaper interview published as the government met to discuss the budget, Witold Kozinski, the central bank's deputy head, said Poland faced a ballooning current account gap and a Czech-style crisis unless the state's books were balanced next year.

Analysts said the remarks showed the National Bank of Poland was seeking a fiscal tightening to accompany its monetary policy efforts to stem domestic demand that has boosted external deficits and showed in troublesome credit expansion.

"This is a signal that the ice may still be thin underneath Poland's macro reforms and the market should pay attention to these extreme statements as they don't come from an extreme man," said David Mars, Director of Emerging Europe and Africa Economic Research at SBC Warburg in London.
But Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told Reuters later on Tuesday that a balanced budget for 1998 was impossible.
"There is no such possibility, in Poland it would require deep budget spending cuts and I do not see such a possibility," Cimoszewicz said in a brief interview.
Analysts said the government's reaction was hardly surprising in view of the parliamentary elections in late September.

Analysts said that Poland could slash its budget gap next year if it cut subsidies to ailing sectors such as mining or agriculture, ended indexation of wages or launched its pension reform, but said that such sweeping moves were not expected ahead of the elections.

"There are many stiff budget expenditures created by an over-socialised approach to some sectors...but this is not likely to change ahead of the elections," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, deputy head of the independent Gdansk Institute for Market Economic Research (IBnGR).
Some said Kozinski's warning to the cabinet might be an attempt to strengthen the position of independent Finance Minister Marek Belka during budgetary discussions.
"In the run-up to the election, Kozinski may be trying to block off any attempts of trying to bully Belka into loosening purse strings," said one London-based analyst.

Belka has said the government would seek a tighter budget next year and signalled the deficit would be at or below two percent, against a 2.8 percent of gross domestic product shortfall planned for 1997, but has not given specific figures.
Analysts said the NBP's restrictive monetary policy in 1997 had proved ineffective in slowing the country's credit boom, which inflated demand for imports and eroded external balance.

"The NBP, seeing it can't realise its goal of reducing credit action, is asking the finance ministry to cut the budget deficit to curb internal demand," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Over the first four months of the year Poland's current account deficit amounted to $2.3 billion, almost $1 billion more than in all of 1996, while the trade deficit soared to $4 billion against $8.2 billion last year.

Credit action grew 13.3 percent in the first five months of 1997, despite fast rising real interest rates, which remained fixed at 22 and 25 percent since last July, despite a six point decline in inflation to May's year-on-year 14.6 percent.
